summary:
Muğla, the province containing Bodrum, Marmaris and Fethiye, stands under the national framework of Turkey. Nothing in the sourced record establishes a Muğla-specific provision on trans people: every measure bearing on a trans visitor to the province is national in scope, and the policing, assembly-ban and document-check patterns documented elsewhere in Turkey apply to Muğla's stations, courts and resort municipalities.

Human Rights Watch reported on 29 October 2025 that a leaked omnibus measure, the 11th Judicial Package, would amend penal-code article 225 so that acts "contrary to biological sex and general morality" carry up to three years' imprisonment, and same-sex engagement or marriage ceremonies up to four years. The same draft would amend civil-code article 40, titled "Changing Sex", raising the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 and adding mandatory infertility evaluation and approval by a government-approved hospital. It would imprison care providers for up to seven years and trans patients for up to three. The document was national-level and contained no province-specific content for Muğla.

Turkey has permitted transgender people to change their legal gender since 1988, but only on condition of sex-reassignment surgery, a medical examination and court permission. There is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, so a visitor who encounters refusals of service, dismissal or police inaction in Muğla has no general statutory discrimination claim to invoke.

Same-sex marriage, civil unions and adoption are not available in Turkey. Because Turkish marriage law determines eligibility by the gender recorded in a person's civil registry rather than by trans status, an individual who has legally changed registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender — the practical relevance for a visitor is that marital status shown on documents is read against the registry entry, not against appearance.

The 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026 with the provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people removed from the bill. The package made symbolic same-sex weddings possible, but those ceremonies carry no legal marital status.

Assembly by LGBT people is a nationwide enforcement target. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 records that the Erdoğan government made anti-LGBT hate speech a core part of its election campaign, that the ninth successive ban on Istanbul Pride week events in June 2023 was accompanied by police arrests of those who attempted to assemble, that authorities regularly and arbitrarily ban other events by LGBT groups, and that local authorities around the country have increasingly cancelled concerts by artists openly supportive of LGBT rights. A trans visitor in Muğla should expect that any visible assembly, Pride event or LGBT-branded performance in the province would be met with the same ban-and-arrest approach applied in Istanbul.
tangentialFactors:
The hostile framing is set at the centre of government rather than left to street prejudice. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 identifies anti-LGBT hate speech as a core element of the ruling party's election campaign, which gives police and municipal officials a political incentive to act against visible LGBT presence in tourist districts.

Content regulation reaches the visitor's own screen. The national broadcast regulator RTÜK has justified fines on digital platforms for LGBT-related content as violating "societal and cultural values", an indication that the restriction regime extends beyond public space into the media consumed while in the country.

The pattern of cancellation is diffuse rather than concentrated in one city. Local authorities around Turkey have increasingly cancelled concerts by artists openly supportive of LGBT rights, so a Muğla resort municipality cancelling an event would be an instance of a national practice rather than a local anomaly.

Drafting versus enacted law remains an open question in the record. The 11th Judicial Package was a leaked draft as of the October 2025 reporting, and the 12th judicial reform package passed in 2026 with its LGBTQ-discriminatory provisions struck; the sources do not state whether any element of the first package was subsequently enacted.

There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination statute covering sexual orientation or gender identity, so workplace, housing, healthcare and service refusals on those grounds have no general statutory prohibition behind them.

Marriage eligibility follows the gender recorded in the civil registry. A person who has legally changed registered gender may marry a partner of the opposite registered gender; same-sex marriage, civil unions and adoption by same-sex couples remain unavailable, and the symbolic same-sex ceremonies introduced by the 12th judicial reform package in 2026 confer no legal marital status.

The pending 11th Judicial Package would, as drafted, raise the age threshold for gender-affirming care to 25, require infertility evaluation and approval by a government-approved hospital, and expose both providers and patients to imprisonment — providers up to seven years, patients up to three.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory reports police practice, document checks, detention figures or violence statistics for Muğla itself; the province's risk profile in this record is inferred entirely from national measures and from enforcement documented in Istanbul. Local Muğla enforcement remains unresolved and unsourced here.

The status of the 11th Judicial Package after the 29 October 2025 reporting is not sourced. Whether its penal-code and civil-code amendments were enacted, amended or dropped is unresolved in this record.

The inventory does not state whether the 2026 removal of discriminatory provisions from the 12th judicial reform package affected any trans-specific provision, nor does it address how the symbolic same-sex wedding provision interacts with document checks or registry entries.

Whether Muğla's resort municipalities have issued their own event bans, and whether the national event-ban pattern has been applied to Pride or trans-specific gatherings in the province, is not sourced and remains unresolved.
